RESULT

GitHub Branch: UI-UX-Create-subscription-plan

1. Shared Understanding

Goal

Create a Subscription Plan page where users can understand their current subscription status, compare Free, Basic, and Pro plans, choose the right subscription action, and buy add-ons for Publish Projects and AI Floor Scanner credits.

Product Intent

The page should help users answer four questions quickly:

  1. What plan am I currently on?
  2. What do Free, Basic, and Pro include?
  3. Should I subscribe, upgrade, or downgrade?
  4. What add-ons can I buy for publishing or AI Floor Scanner usage?

The page should feel like the dashboard and profile pages: calm, workspace-native, rounded, structured, and direct. It should not feel like a marketing landing page.

In Scope

  • Subscription status summary.
  • Free, Basic, and Pro plan price list.
  • Plan comparison details:
    • Plan name.
    • Price.
    • Publish project limit.
    • AI Floor Scanner credit amount.
    • Export to GeoJSON availability.
    • View details link to the pricing plan page.
    • Subscribe, Upgrade, or Downgrade button.
  • Add-on Publish price list:
    • Extra Publish Project.
    • Temporary Publish Pass.
    • Only visible when the user has an active subscription plan.
  • Add-on AI Floor Scanner Credit price list:
    • Always visible for subscribed and unsubscribed users.
  • Subscription status states:
    • Current subscription plan.
    • Renewal or expiration date.
    • Subscribed.
    • Pending unsubscribed.
    • Unsubscribed.
  • Non-technical design guidance for UI UX Pro Max.

Out of Scope

  • Full checkout flow.
  • Billing address editing.
  • Card management.
  • Invoice history.
  • Receipt downloads.
  • Tax calculation.
  • Team or organization subscription management.
  • Deep pricing-plan marketing page content.

2. Dashboard and Profile Style Source of Truth

The Subscription Plan page should use the same workspace shell and visual rhythm as the dashboard and profile page.

Shell Pattern

Use the same layout family:

  • Sticky MapThru top navigation.
  • Left sidebar on large screens.
  • Subscription Plan active in the sidebar.
  • Main content column.
  • Right rail on wide screens.
  • Soft ambient brand wash behind the page.
  • Wide workspace container.
  • Responsive stacking on smaller screens.

Visual Language

Preserve these style cues:

  • Rounded-xl and rounded-2xl surfaces.
  • Soft borders.
  • Semi-transparent card surfaces.
  • Muted helper text.
  • Small icon-led labels.
  • Primary color accents for the selected or current plan.
  • Amber treatment for upgrade prompts, expiring plans, or attention states.
  • Destructive or caution styling only for downgrade or unsubscribed states.
  • Gradient primary button for the strongest recommended action.
  • Compact headings and clean comparison cards.

What the Page Should Not Become

  • Not a hero landing page.
  • Not a dense spreadsheet copied into the UI.
  • Not a checkout page.
  • Not a modal-only experience.
  • Not a one-column wall of prices.

3. Recommended Page Direction

Recommended Approach: Account-Native Plan Management Page

Create a dedicated Subscription Plan page inside the dashboard shell:

  1. Top status summary explains the user's current subscription state.
  2. Three plan cards compare Free, Basic, and Pro.
  3. Add-on Publish section appears only for subscribed users.
  4. Add-on AI Floor Scanner Credit section always appears.
  5. Right rail summarizes current plan, renewal/expiration date, and recommended next action.

This approach is recommended because the page is both a comparison page and an account-management page. Users should see pricing clearly, but the first priority is helping them manage their current MapThru subscription.

Alternatives Considered

Alternative A: Full pricing table

This would show many details at once, but it may feel too dense inside the dashboard. Plan cards are easier to scan.

Alternative B: Checkout-first plan page

This would push users toward payment quickly, but it would hide important plan comparison and status context.

Alternative C: Split plans and add-ons into separate pages

This would reduce page length, but users need to understand plans and add-ons together because add-ons depend on subscription status.

5. Page Layout

Header Area

Purpose: Introduce the page and show the user's subscription context.

Suggested content:

  • Small context label: Subscription plan
  • Main title: Plans and add-ons
  • Supporting text: Compare plans, manage your subscription, and add more publishing or AI scanner capacity.
  • Optional compact status chip: Current plan: Free, Basic, or Pro.

Subscription Status Summary

Place near the top, before the price cards.

The summary should show:

  • Current subscription plan.
  • Subscription status.
  • Renewal date or expiration date.
  • Pending unsubscribed state when cancellation is scheduled.
  • Unsubscribed state when the user no longer has an active plan.

Suggested status labels:

  • Subscribed.
  • Pending unsubscribe.
  • Unsubscribed.
  • Free plan.

Suggested examples:

  • Current plan: Basic.

  • Status: Subscribed.

  • Renews on: August 1, 2026.

  • Current plan: Pro.

  • Status: Pending unsubscribe.

  • Access ends on: August 1, 2026.

  • Current plan: Free.

  • Status: Unsubscribed.

  • No renewal date.

Plan Cards Section

Show Free, Basic, and Pro as three cards in one responsive section.

Each card should include:

  • Plan name.
  • Price.
  • Publish project limit.
  • AI Floor Scanner amount.
  • Export to GeoJSON availability.
  • View details link.
  • Plan action button.

Recommended card emphasis:

  • Current plan card gets a clear "Current plan" badge.
  • Pro can receive a subtle "Best for teams" or "Most capacity" badge if product wants a recommendation.
  • Free should stay calm and not look like an error.
  • Downgrade action should look less dominant than Subscribe or Upgrade.

Add-On Publish Section

Only show this section if the user has an active subscribed plan.

Show:

  • Extra Publish Project.
  • Temporary Publish Pass.
  • Price.
  • Short use case.
  • Buy add-on button.

If the user is Free or unsubscribed, hide this section or replace it with a small note in the plan cards explaining that publish add-ons become available after subscribing.

Add-On AI Floor Scanner Credit Section

Always show this section.

Show:

  • 5 credits for $9.
  • 15 credits for $24.
  • 50 credits for $69.
  • 150 credits for $179.
  • Note that these add-on credits do not combine with monthly credit accumulation.
  • Buy credits button on each option.

Right Rail

On wide screens, use a right rail for:

  • Current subscription status.
  • Renewal or access end date.
  • Current publish usage, if available.
  • Current AI Floor Scanner credit balance, if available.
  • Short note about monthly included credits.
  • Primary recommended action:
    • Subscribe when user is Free.
    • Upgrade when user is Basic.
    • Manage plan when user is Pro.

6. Plan Action Button Rules

The plan action button has three modes.

Subscribe

Use when the user has not subscribed yet.

Example:

  • User is on Free or unsubscribed.
  • Basic card button: Subscribe.
  • Pro card button: Subscribe.

Upgrade

Use when the target plan is higher than the user's current plan.

Examples:

  • Current plan is Free, target plan is Basic or Pro: Upgrade or Subscribe depending on product language.
  • Current plan is Basic, target plan is Pro: Upgrade.

Recommended product language:

  • Use Subscribe for users with no paid plan.
  • Use Upgrade for paid users moving to a higher plan.

Downgrade

Use when the target plan is lower than the user's current paid plan.

Examples:

  • Current plan is Pro, target plan is Basic: Downgrade.
  • Current plan is Pro or Basic, target plan is Free: Downgrade.

Downgrade should be visually quieter than Upgrade. It should be clear, but not styled as the recommended action.

Current Plan

The current plan card should not show Subscribe, Upgrade, or Downgrade.

Recommended button or label:

  • Current plan.
  • Manage plan.

Use "Manage plan" if the user can change renewal or cancellation settings from this page.

7. Subscription Status States

Subscribed

Meaning:

  • User has an active paid plan.

Display:

  • Current plan.
  • Status: Subscribed.
  • Renewal date.
  • Active plan badge.

Pending Unsubscribed

Meaning:

  • User has canceled renewal, but still has access until the end date.

Display:

  • Current plan.
  • Status: Pending unsubscribe.
  • Access ends on date.
  • Keep plan benefits visible until expiration.
  • Offer a "Resume subscription" or "Keep plan" action if supported.

Unsubscribed

Meaning:

  • User does not have an active paid plan.

Display:

  • Current plan: Free.
  • Status: Unsubscribed.
  • No renewal date.
  • Subscribe buttons on paid plans.
  • Hide add-on Publish section.
  • Keep AI Floor Scanner credit add-ons visible.

Free Plan

Meaning:

  • User is using free access without a paid subscription.

Display:

  • Current plan: Free.
  • Free benefits.
  • Subscribe buttons on Basic and Pro.
  • No add-on Publish section.

8. UI/UX Master Data For UI UX Pro Max

Navigation Pattern

Pattern: Dashboard shell with left sidebar, main content, and right rail.
Active navigation item: Subscription Plan.
Entry points: Dashboard sidebar, profile page subscription card, billing page, upgrade prompt.
Exit points: Pricing plan details page, checkout, billing page, dashboard.

Screen Inventory

Screen ID Screen name Navigation type Entry from Exits to
S-01 Subscription Plan Sidebar page Dashboard, Profile, Billing, Upgrade prompt Pricing details, Checkout, Billing, Dashboard

S-01: Subscription Plan

  • Purpose: Let users compare subscription plans, understand current status, and buy plan or add-on capacity.
  • Key elements:
    • Dashboard shell.
    • Subscription status summary.
    • Free, Basic, and Pro plan cards.
    • Plan action buttons.
    • Add-On Publish section.
    • Add-On AI Floor Scanner Credit section.
    • Right rail summary.
  • Primary action:
    • Subscribe, Upgrade, or Manage plan based on user state.
  • Required states:
    • Default.
    • Loading.
    • Free/unsubscribed.
    • Subscribed.
    • Pending unsubscribe.
    • Error.
    • Add-on unavailable.
    • Add-on available.
  • Design implications:
    • The current plan must be instantly recognizable.
    • Paid plan options should be easy to compare without reading dense tables.
    • Add-ons should feel secondary to the main plans but still purchasable.
    • AI Floor Scanner credits are always visible because both free and paid users can buy them.

New Components To Design

Component Purpose
Subscription status summary Shows plan, status, renewal or expiration date.
Plan comparison card Shows each plan's price, key limits, details link, and action.
Plan action button Supports Subscribe, Upgrade, Downgrade, Current plan, and Manage plan states.
Add-on publish card Shows publish add-ons available only to subscribed users.
Add-on AI credit card Shows credit bundles available to all users.
Subscription right rail summary Shows compact current plan, usage, dates, and next action.

Interaction And Motion

Interaction Behavior
Select plan action Button shows working state and routes user to checkout or plan-management flow.
View details Opens pricing plan page for that plan.
Buy publish add-on Starts add-on purchase flow for subscribed users.
Buy AI credits Starts credit purchase flow for all users.
Downgrade Uses calmer button treatment and may require confirmation.
Pending unsubscribe Shows access-end date and optionally offers resume action.

Accessibility Requirements

  • Plan cards must have clear headings.
  • Prices must be readable and not only communicated by color.
  • Current plan must be announced as text, not only highlighted visually.
  • Buttons must clearly say Subscribe, Upgrade, Downgrade, Manage plan, or Current plan.
  • Add-on availability must be explained in text.
  • The page must be usable by keyboard.
  • Responsive layout must keep plan cards readable on small screens.

10. Key User Flows

Flow A: Free User Subscribes

  1. User opens Subscription Plan from the sidebar.
  2. Status summary shows Free plan or Unsubscribed.
  3. User compares Free, Basic, and Pro cards.
  4. User clicks Subscribe on Basic or Pro.
  5. User moves to checkout or subscription flow.

Flow B: Basic User Upgrades To Pro

  1. User opens Subscription Plan.
  2. Status summary shows Basic and renewal date.
  3. Basic card is marked Current plan.
  4. Pro card shows Upgrade.
  5. User clicks Upgrade.

Flow C: Pro User Downgrades

  1. User opens Subscription Plan.
  2. Status summary shows Pro and renewal date.
  3. Basic or Free card shows Downgrade.
  4. User clicks Downgrade.
  5. Page clearly warns or confirms the downgrade if required.

Flow D: Subscribed User Buys Publish Add-On

  1. User opens Subscription Plan while subscribed.
  2. Add-On Publish section is visible.
  3. User chooses Extra Publish Project or Temporary Publish Pass.
  4. User clicks Buy add-on.

Flow E: Any User Buys AI Floor Scanner Credits

  1. User opens Subscription Plan.
  2. AI Floor Scanner Credit section is visible.
  3. User chooses 5, 15, 50, or 150 credits.
  4. User clicks Buy credits.

Flow F: Pending Unsubscribe User Reviews Access

  1. User opens Subscription Plan.
  2. Status summary shows Pending unsubscribe.
  3. Page shows access end date.
  4. User can decide whether to resume, subscribe again, or wait until expiration.

11. States And Edge Cases

Loading States

  • Loading subscription status.
  • Loading plan prices.
  • Starting subscription.
  • Starting upgrade.
  • Starting downgrade.
  • Buying add-on.
  • Loading add-on availability.

Empty States

  • No paid subscription.
  • No renewal date.
  • No publish add-ons available because user is not subscribed.
  • No AI credit balance available.

Error States

  • Subscription status cannot load.
  • Pricing cannot load.
  • Checkout cannot start.
  • Upgrade cannot start.
  • Downgrade cannot start.
  • Add-on purchase cannot start.

Edge Cases

  • User is Free but has purchased AI credits.
  • User is pending unsubscribe but still has plan benefits until expiration.
  • User is Pro and cannot upgrade further.
  • User is Free and cannot downgrade.
  • User has Basic but publish add-ons are unavailable due to payment issue.
  • User has expired subscription but still sees old plan name.
  • Spreadsheet pricing changes and UI needs updated values.

12. Acceptance Criteria

Layout And Style

  • Subscription Plan page uses the same dashboard shell as src/app/dashboard/page.tsx.
  • Top MapThru navigation is present.
  • Left sidebar is present on large screens.
  • Subscription Plan is the active sidebar item.
  • Main content uses dashboard/profile-style rounded cards.
  • Right rail summarizes current plan, dates, and next action on wide screens.
  • Page is written as an account workspace page, not a marketing landing page.

Subscription Status

  • User can see current subscription plan.
  • User can see subscribed, pending unsubscribe, unsubscribed, or free status.
  • User can see renewal date when subscribed.
  • User can see access end or expiration date when pending unsubscribe or expired.
  • Status summary appears before the plan cards.

Plan Price List

  • Free, Basic, and Pro plans are visible.
  • Each plan shows name and price.
  • Each plan shows publish project limit.
  • Each plan shows AI Floor Scanner amount.
  • Each plan shows Export to GeoJSON availability.
  • Each plan has a View details link to the pricing plan page.
  • Each non-current plan has the correct Subscribe, Upgrade, or Downgrade action.
  • Current plan is clearly marked.

Add-On Publish Price List

  • Extra Publish Project and Temporary Publish Pass are shown only when the user has an active subscription.
  • Each add-on shows price and use case.
  • Free or unsubscribed users do not see purchasable publish add-on cards.
  • Free or unsubscribed users may see a short note that publish add-ons require a subscription.

Add-On AI Floor Scanner Credits

  • AI Floor Scanner credit add-ons are always visible.
  • 5, 15, 50, and 150 credit bundles are shown.
  • Each credit bundle shows price.
  • Page explains that these credits do not combine with monthly credit accumulation.
  • Each credit bundle has a buy action.

Button Modes

  • Subscribe appears when the user has no paid subscription.
  • Upgrade appears when the user chooses a higher plan.
  • Downgrade appears when the user chooses a lower plan.
  • Current plan is not shown as Subscribe, Upgrade, or Downgrade.
  • Downgrade is visually quieter than Subscribe or Upgrade.

13. QA Scenarios

  1. Free user opens the page and sees Free as current plan.
  2. Free user sees Subscribe on Basic and Pro.
  3. Basic user sees Basic as current plan.
  4. Basic user sees Upgrade on Pro.
  5. Basic user sees Downgrade on Free.
  6. Pro user sees Pro as current plan.
  7. Pro user sees Downgrade on Basic and Free.
  8. Pending unsubscribe user sees access end date.
  9. Unsubscribed user sees paid plan Subscribe buttons.
  10. Subscribed user sees Add-On Publish section.
  11. Free user does not see purchasable Add-On Publish cards.
  12. Any user sees AI Floor Scanner credit bundles.
  13. View details link is available on each plan card.
  14. Current plan is identifiable without relying on color alone.
  15. Page remains readable on mobile and desktop.

14. Open Questions

Question Recommended default Owner
Should Free be treated as a plan or only as an unsubscribed state? Treat Free as a visible plan card and as the default current plan for unsubscribed users. Product
Should paid prices show monthly/yearly toggle? Show both monthly and yearly prices in each card for now. Product / Design
Should Pro be visually recommended? Add a subtle "Most capacity" badge, not a loud marketing banner. Product / Design
Should downgrade require confirmation? Yes, because it may reduce limits and access. Product
Should add-on publish appear for Basic and Pro only? Yes, only active subscribed users should see purchasable publish add-ons. Product
Should AI credits be purchasable by Free users? Yes, always visible and purchasable. Product
Where should View details open? Pricing plan page. Product

15. Risks

Risk Impact Mitigation
Page becomes too dense with plans and add-ons. Users may miss key actions. Use plan cards first, add-ons below, and right rail summary.
Button mode is confusing. Users may not understand subscribe vs upgrade vs downgrade. Use explicit button labels and current-plan badge.
Add-on visibility is unclear. Free users may wonder where publish add-ons went. Show a short note that publish add-ons require subscription.
Spreadsheet prices change. UI may become outdated. Treat spreadsheet as pricing source of truth.
Downgrade feels like a primary action. Users may accidentally reduce plan. Use quieter visual treatment and optional confirmation.
Page drifts from dashboard/profile style. Product feels inconsistent. Reuse dashboard shell, sidebar, rounded cards, right rail, and muted helper text.

16. Design Summary

The Subscription Plan page should be a dashboard-native plan management page. It should show the user's current subscription status first, then help users compare Free, Basic, and Pro, then show add-ons in the right availability order: Publish add-ons only for subscribed users, AI Floor Scanner credits for everyone. UI UX Pro Max should design this as an account workspace layout, using the same MapThru dashboard and profile visual language rather than a public marketing pricing page.

RESULT

Subscription page implemented at src/app/subscription/page.tsx. Your Subscription summary (plan/renewal/credits + status: Subscribed/Free/Payment due/Pending unsubscribe), Compare plans (Free/Basic/Pro feature matrix, Monthly/Yearly toggle, rank-aware CTAs: Current/Manage/Downgrade/Subscribe/Upgrade), Add-on Publish (subscribed-only), AI Floor Scanner credit packs (always, Best value). Right rail: anchors + current-plan card. Wired to billing status + checkout/portal; add-on/credit buys are checkout stubs.

Goal

Create an Invoice page where users can view their invoice history in a clear table, sorted by the latest date first, with status tabs for All, Paid, Pending, and Overdue. Each invoice row should show date, product, type, amount, status, and a download button.

Product Intent

The page should help users quickly answer:

  1. What invoices do I have?
  2. Which invoices are paid, pending, or overdue?
  3. What product or purchase does each invoice belong to?
  4. Can I download the invoice immediately?

The page should feel like the dashboard, profile, billing, and subscription pages: workspace-native, calm, rounded, table-focused, and easy to scan.

In Scope

  • Invoice list table.
  • Default sorting by latest date first.
  • Invoice status tabs:
    • All.
    • Paid.
    • Pending.
    • Overdue.
  • Counter inside each status tab, matching the dashboard tab-counter pattern.
  • Table columns:
    • Date.
    • Product.
    • Type.
    • Amount.
    • Status.
    • Download.
  • Invoice type values:
    • Subscription.
    • Extra Publish.
    • Publish Pass.
    • AI Credits.
  • Invoice status values:
    • Paid.
    • Pending.
    • Overdue.
  • Download button for each row.
  • Empty, loading, filtered-empty, and error states.
  • Non-technical UI/UX data source for Claude's UI UX Pro Max skill.

Out of Scope

  • Creating invoices.
  • Editing invoice data.
  • Payment retry flow.
  • Refund management.
  • Tax detail editing.
  • Billing address editing.
  • Card management.
  • Full invoice PDF design.

The Invoice page should use the same workspace shell and visual rhythm as the dashboard and account pages.

Use the same layout family:

  • Sticky MapThru top navigation.
  • Left sidebar on large screens.
  • Invoice active in the sidebar.
  • Main content column.
  • Optional right rail on wide screens.
  • Soft ambient brand wash behind the page.
  • Wide workspace container.
  • Responsive stacking on smaller screens.

Visual Language

Preserve these dashboard cues:

  • Rounded-xl and rounded-2xl surfaces.
  • Soft borders.
  • Semi-transparent card or table container.
  • Muted helper text.
  • Compact headings.
  • Tab list with counters, matching the dashboard project-status filter tabs.
  • Primary color for the active tab.
  • Green or success treatment for Paid.
  • Amber treatment for Pending.
  • Destructive or caution treatment for Overdue.
  • Icon button or compact button for Download.

  • Not a marketing page.
  • Not a checkout page.
  • Not a dense accounting dashboard.
  • Not a card grid when a table is clearer.
  • Not a full invoice preview page.

3. Recommended Page Direction

Recommended Approach: Table-First Invoice History Page

Create a dedicated Invoice page inside the dashboard shell:

  1. Header introduces invoice history.
  2. A compact summary shows total invoices and key counts.
  3. Status tabs filter the table by All, Paid, Pending, and Overdue.
  4. Invoice table lists invoices sorted by newest date first.
  5. Each row has a Download button.
  6. Right rail can summarize invoice status counts or billing links on wide screens.

This is recommended because invoice history is naturally tabular. Users need to scan dates, amounts, status, and download actions quickly.

Alternatives Considered

Alternative A: Invoice cards

Cards would be more visual, but they make it harder to compare dates, amounts, and statuses across many invoices.

Alternative B: Separate pages for each invoice status

Separate pages would add navigation weight. Status tabs are faster and match the dashboard pattern.

Alternative C: Full financial dashboard

This would be too heavy for the current goal. Users only need a clean invoice list and downloads.

Goal

Add shape creation tools to the 2D editor toolbar so users can mark physical indoor objects such as tables, chairs, counters, fixtures, equipment, shelves, and other occupied spaces inside rooms.

Shapes are not rooms and are not decorative stickers. They represent non-walkable indoor objects in the Digital Twin, and direction lines should route around them instead of passing through them.

Scope

  • Add a Shapes dropdown to the 2D toolbar near Area, Point, and Safety tools.
  • Include Rectangle, Circle, and Polygon tools in the dropdown.
  • Support shape creation directly in the 2D panel.
  • Support Esc cancellation while drawing.
  • Support Shift precision behavior for rectangle and polygon creation.
  • Support selecting, moving, resizing, reshaping, deleting, undoing, and redoing completed shapes.
  • Treat completed shapes as non-walkable route obstacles.
  • Add a clear visibility option: Show shapes.

Recommended Toolbar Placement

Recommended 2D toolbar order:

  1. Wall
  2. Curve
  3. Window
  4. Area
  5. Shapes
  6. Point
  7. Safety
  8. Undo
  9. Redo

Tool Behavior

Rectangle

  • User selects Rectangle from Shapes.
  • User clicks first corner.
  • User clicks opposite corner.
  • Holding Shift creates a 1:1 square.
  • Esc cancels the unfinished rectangle.
  • After creation, user can adjust length, width, and position.
  • Rectangle blocks direction lines from passing through it.

Circle

  • User selects Circle from Shapes.
  • User clicks center or starting point.
  • User clicks radius point.
  • Circle starts as a 1:1 round shape.
  • Esc cancels the unfinished circle.
  • After creation, user can resize width and height, allowing the circle to become an oval.
  • Circle or oval blocks direction lines from passing through it.

Polygon

  • User selects Polygon from Shapes.
  • User clicks to place multiple points.
  • Polygon completes when the start and end points meet.
  • Holding Shift enables Snap to Grid for point placement.
  • Esc cancels the unfinished polygon.
  • After creation, user can move points, rearrange the object shape, and move the whole polygon.
  • Polygon blocks direction lines from passing through it.

Summary

Data layer for the Add Panorama tool (#225): read a GoThru/TourMkr virtual tour link and turn it into a list of panoramas (names, positions, viewing angles, thumbnail, 360 image) ready to place on the map.

docs/superpowers/brainstorming/2026-07-14-add-pano-data-fetching-brainstorming.md

The reading pipeline (6 steps)

  • Trim the key from the link — path segment starting with F1/G1, excluding the prefix (existing extractTourKey)
  • Resolve the tour: GET /v1/internal/tours/{tourKey} → id_user, cid, tour_id

  • Per pano: open {pano_id}.json for thumbnail + 360 image (and children)
  • Hand to the Add Panorama tool (#225), routed by whether the pano has a map position

Five map types → unified record

Unified record: panoId, name, mapType, x, y, lat, lng, theta, phi, fov, radius, thumbnailUrl, imageUrl, children[]

Map type Position Placement (per #225)
Floor Map x/y Import & Apply Location (alignment overlay)
Journey Map x/y (+ children, recursive) Import & Apply Location
Mapbox lat/lng Import & Apply Location (pre-placed)
Splash Map none (angles only) Import → center cluster
No Map Plugin none (angles only) Import → center cluster

issues.main_description_html:
Demo by Developer

Before

video-859-before.mp4

After

video-859-after.mp4

Description:

Update CSS positioning and dynamic viewport offset for location detail popups on mobile devices to prevent top header bar overlap.

Acceptance Criteria:

  1. Adjust modal top offset / CSS safe-area inset calculations to account for the total height of top floating control bars.
  2. Ensure the modal close button ("X") remains un-obscured, fully visible, and clickable on both Mobile Safari and Mobile Chrome.
  3. Verify z-index stack hierarchy so floating header controls and modal elements do not visually collide or block user inputs.

RESULT

PreviewControls is absolute left-4 top-4 z-20 with flex-wrap. At phone width it takes two rows and its bottom edge lands at 160px. The visitor info card was pinned at a constant top-4, so it opened at 64px — under the toolbar, which outranks it (z-20 over z-10).

Measured on /preview/<id> at 390x844 against the real project:

before after
toolbar bottom 160 160
card top 64 168
toolbar controls over the card 6 0
a tap on the card's title reaches "Direction" the card

All six controls — Back to Editor, Search Area, Direction, Event, Building, Floor — painted across the card's header. A tap meant for the card's title reached the Direction button, which opens the Direction panel and clears the selection, so the card the visitor was reading disappeared.

Note on AC2. The close button was already clickable in this project: row 1 of the toolbar ends at x=208 and the X sits at x≈303, so it falls in a gap between controls. It is the card's header that was buried, not the X. AC1 and AC3 were both failing.

Note on AC1's safe-area insets. Not involved. There is no env(safe-area-inset-*) anywhere in src/, and layout.tsx exports no viewport, so without viewport-fit=cover the insets resolve to 0. The cause is the toolbar's height alone.

Fix

The panels on the left already start below a measured clearance (panelTop, #811). The card now takes the same number through a new topOffset prop, and drives its position and height cap from it:

top-(--toolbar-clear)  max-h-[calc(100%_-_var(--toolbar-clear)_-_1rem)]
xl:top-4               xl:max-h-[calc(100%_-_2rem)]

Confined to below xl on purpose. From there up the two never meet, and top-4 right-14 is the approved placement from #211, whose gap above the card once rendered as a black compositing artifact over the WebGL canvas in Chromium. A breakpoint rather than a second resize listener, because whether they collide at all is a width question — the answer #851 gave the search panel.

Fixed along the way

The height cap moved from 100dvh - var(--editor-topbar-h) - 2rem to the card's own containing block. The overlay only insets itself by the navbar when standalone, so the old cap was 48px short on the public viewer, inside an embed, and over the editor. At 1440 the card is now 868px tall instead of 816.

Verification

Measured in Chromium at 360 / 390 / 1279 / 1440: the card clears the toolbar at every width below xl, holds top: 16px and calc(100% - 32px) from xl up, and the close button hit-tests to itself throughout.

Two 390x844 60fps recordings in .playwright-mcp/demo/859/ — video-859-before.mp4 and video-859-after.mp4, the same scenario against both builds. The scenario asserts on the after run, so the recording doubles as a check.

Four unit tests cover the wiring: the measured offset reaches the element, xl:top-4 survives, the height cap is no longer expressed in 100dvh, and the default is the plain top-4 inset.

The #211 compositing artifact does not recur — the gap between toolbar and card renders the map. Verified on Chromium/Vulkan on Linux; not yet checked on iOS Safari.

Residual

The xl cut is a breakpoint, not a measurement. The toolbar measured 647px wide here; on a 1280–1400px screen with much longer building and floor names it could still reach the card and would not be pushed clear. Same residual #851 accepted when it chose lg.

issues.display_title: Issue #569: Collab never syncs canvasData.buildings — a peer's autosave deletes building records
issues.main_description_html:
Found while verifying the PRD #536 gap fixes (#561–#566). Pre-existing, and it silently destroys data.

Description

A collab snapshot is one level's LevelData as JSON (src/lib/collab/sync.ts) — grep -rn buildings src/lib/collab/ returns zero hits. There is no channel for the buildings array or for the per-building mapTransform.

sync.ts deliberately carries buildingId across a snapshot ("Level identity is store-only too (#536)"), which shows the level stamp was considered — the building records were not.

FloorplanEditor.tsx applies a peer snapshot as store.setCanvasData({ ...data, levels: nextLevels }) where data is the local canvasData, so a peer keeps its own stale buildings. That peer's next edit flips hasUnsavedChanges, and the editor autosaves its whole canvasData two seconds later — overwriting the other editor's buildings server-side.

Result: a building record and its placement disappear, while levels stamped with it keep a buildingId pointing at a record that no longer exists. (The orphan case is now survivable — groupLevelsByBuilding falls those levels back to the default building as of #566 — but the building and its placement are still gone.)

Fix direction

Either broadcast building records as their own message type, or stop letting an autosave write the whole canvasData when only levels were synced. Whichever lands, a peer must not be able to delete another's building by editing a floor.

Acceptance Criteria

  • Adding, renaming, or deleting a building propagates to collaborators
  • A peer editing a floor cannot drop another peer's building records
  • Per-building placement survives a collab session
  • Unit test: applying a peer level snapshot preserves local building records
